{"concepts_used":["GC-0012","GC-0015","GC-0014","GC-0001","GC-0002","GC-0004","GC-0071","GC-0064"],"decline_reason":"","declined":false,"citations":[{"ref":"TMM/Part14/6/6/4/4","quote":"A specification may be restricted, or an endorsement limiting the use of the trade mark may be entered, to ensure that in use the trade mark will not be deceptive or confusing."},{"ref":"TMA1995/s43","quote":"An application for the registration of a trade mark in respect of particular goods or services must be rejected if, because of some connotation that the trade mark or a sign contained in the trade mark has, the use of the trade mark in relation to those goods or services would be likely to deceive or cause confusion."},{"ref":"TMM/Part29/9/9/5","quote":"An applicant will be able to overcome a geographical section 43 objection by agreeing to a condition of registration or a specification amendment which removes the likelihood of consumers being deceived or confused. This is the sole criterion for conditions or limitations applied in order to overcome grounds for rejection raised under section 43. The condition of registration or specification amendment must directly address the connotation in the trade mark."},{"ref":"TMM/Part26/4/4/3~2","quote":"The more closely related the goods on the one hand and the services on the other, the greater the potential for confusion as to whether they originate from the same person."}],"answer":"Yes, in principle—but distinguish confusion arising from the mark’s connotation from confusion between competing marks.

• Manual practice: a specification may be restricted, or an endorsement limiting use entered, to ensure that use is not deceptive or confusing [TMM/Part14/6/6/4/4]. For section 43, the Manual says the restriction must remove the likelihood of deception or confusion and directly address the mark’s connotation; it expressly describes specification amendment as a way to overcome a geographical section 43 objection [TMM/Part29/9/9/5].

• Act: section 43 requires rejection where a connotation of the mark or a sign within it makes use on the specified goods or services likely to deceive or cause confusion. This statutory test is distinct from the Manual’s practice concerning restrictions [TMA1995/s43].

• Closely related goods and services: in its discussion of section 44, the Manual explains that closer relatedness increases the potential for confusion about a common source [TMM/Part26/4/4/3~2]. However, the supplied passages do not establish when a specification restriction would overcome that section 44 conflict. The section 43 restriction guidance should therefore not be treated as a guarantee that restricting the specification resolves confusion between competing marks."}
